note: What each bridge host revision added. See scripts/check-host-revision.js.
A host declares the revision it has reached; every channel it answers must
be introduced here at or below that revision, and every channel introduced
at or below it must be answered. Adding a channel without a ledger entry
fails the build, which is the point.

revisions.summary: Baseline â€” the bridge as both hosts implemented it when over-the-air bundle delivery was designed.

The page tells the host how it looks: set-appearance drives the status bar, and splash-shown says the web splash has painted. Both are sends, so an older host logs them rather than hanging â€” but a bundle gated on the appearance channel would leave the clock unreadable on a host that ignores it.

Android answers the over-the-air update channels, so the shared update modal works on mobile. "Install" rebuilds the WebView rather than restarting anything â€” see homerun-mobile/docs/ota-bundles.md.

Android answers the two system-chrome channels. set-appearance sets the status-bar glyph style from the page theme; splash-shown is answered and deliberately does nothing, because the launch screen is a themed window background Android replaces on first frame.

iOS answers the over-the-air update channels. Same two as Android gained at revision 3, arriving later because the iOS host is behind â€” the ledger records what each host answers, not when the feature was designed.

Both hosts play haptics. The page sends what the user just did â€” selection, navigate, commit, success, warning, error â€” and each host maps it onto its own generators. Both arrive in one revision because the contract and the vocabulary landed together, unlike the staggered pairs above. Android jumps 4 to 6: revision 5 introduced nothing for it.

Both hosts can run an OAuth redirect in a real browser. Google refuses to authenticate inside an embedded WebView, so sign-in with Google or Apple cannot happen in our own page; the host opens a system browser and reports the callback URL back. The host knows nothing about OAuth â€” PKCE, the authorize URL and the code exchange stay in the shared UI.

Android can sign in to a Minecraft account. Minigame stats are keyed on a Minecraft uuid and every read of them takes one as input, so a phone could only ever show a signed-in user zero of their own numbers. No new channels: the three invokes and two events already existed and were re-tiered onto the `minecraftAccount` capability, so this is a host learning to answer what the contract already described. The flow is OAuth device code against the public Xbox client rather than a redirect, because the only redirect that client accepts is a Microsoft-hosted page a phone cannot intercept without an App Link it cannot verify. iOS is unchanged and still reports the capability false.

Android receives remote push. Firebase Cloud Messaging, behind the new `remotePush` capability: the host answers the three push:* invokes (permission state, the prompt, the FCM token) and emits push:token-changed and push:opened. The host owns only what must be native — the OS permission sheet and the token Firebase mints; registering that token with the API is the shared UI's job over the user's own JWT, the same split as social sign-in, so no identity passes through the host. push:opened rides the ready-handshake queue because a cold-start tap arrives before the page exists — the same shape as the cold-start deep link. iOS is unchanged, still reports remotePush false, and gains these at its own M4.
